title: The Tariff With Eight Exceptions
framing: On January 14 the President signed the semiconductor tariff the Commerce Department had spent nine months investigating: 25 percent on advanced computing chips, in force at midnight. It does not apply to chips bound for American data centers, research, startups, repairs, consumer devices, civil industry or government — eight exemptions, which is to say nearly every buyer in the country. The proclamation promises a "Phase 2" of broader tariffs at "significant" rates and a "tariff offset program" for companies that build here; the Secretary has ninety days to report on negotiations. The next day Washington and Taipei signed the trade agreement the tariff was written to enforce: Taiwan's chipmakers commit at least $250 billion of new American fabs, Taiwan's government guarantees $250 billion more in credit, Taiwan's tariff is capped at 15 percent, and a company building a fab here may import two and a half times its planned capacity duty-free while it builds. On CNBC the Commerce Secretary said the aim is to move 40 percent of Taiwan's chipmaking to the United States. The same day TSMC told investors it will spend $52 to $56 billion this year, that its second Arizona fab is built and will be tooled this year for volume production in the second half of 2027, that a third is under construction and a fourth is in permitting — on top of the $165 billion it pledged in March 2025 and the $6.6 billion the CHIPS Act awarded it. The first Arizona fab has been making 4-nanometer chips since 2024. The United States makes about a tenth of the chips it uses. The Supreme Court heard argument in November 2025 on whether the emergency tariffs were ever the President's to impose, and has not ruled.
prompt: Twenty-five percent on foreign chips, and almost nobody here pays it. Is that a tariff, or a deal?

previousFraming.prompt: Tariff escalation and semiconductor reshoring collide. Both sides claim vindication.
previousFraming.framing: Broad tariff escalation coincided with TSMC's Arizona fabrication plant reaching production milestones. The policy debate split between tariff advocates and industrial-policy advocates, both claiming the reshoring as vindication. Neither side engaged the deeper supply chain — EUV lithography machines from ASML in the Netherlands remain the binding constraint.

objectLean.stated: 25 percent on foreign chips — build here or pay
objectLean.operative: a narrow duty on AI chips with eight exemptions covering nearly every domestic buyer, paired with a Taiwan deal that trades a 15% cap and duty-free allowances for $250B of fabs

goodFaith.text: Reshoring yes. Tariffs no. Industrial policy is the tool.

coalition.text: The framework failed. I'm not sure tariffs didn't work.

badFaith.text: It's a regressive tax with a nationalist paint job.

goodFaith.text: Tariffs distort prices, invite retaliation, and surrender leverage.

coalition.text: Comparative advantage was right on aggregate, wrong on distribution.

badFaith.text: Markets were already reshoring. Politicians just want the photo.

goodFaith.text: Cheap goods meant exploited workers. The friction is overdue.

coalition.text: The thing I wanted is happening for the wrong reasons.

badFaith.text: Reshoring is hegemony maintenance. We're forcing the transfer.

goodFaith.text: Thirty years of 'inevitable.' Now it's 'too expensive.' For who?

coalition.text: I believe in the direction. I'm not sure who's steering.

badFaith.text: Bring it all back. Every factory. Every job. American.

LF.text: The left is distinguishing between industrial policy and tariffs — the CHIPS Act produced TSMC Arizona; the consumer tariffs are a regressive tax that funds nothing and builds nothing.

LC.text: The left spent fifteen years defending the multilateral framework and is watching the framework's predictions miss while a tariff-plus-subsidy mess produces the reshoring the framework said it would deliver.

LD.text: The left is reading the tariffs as American economic warfare on the Global South, treating reshoring as hegemony maintenance and arguing for cheap goods produced under conditions it would call exploitation if they happened here.

RF.text: The right is correct that decades of offshoring created real distributional harm — comparative advantage was right about aggregate welfare and wrong about distribution, and the adjustment mechanisms never got built.

RC.text: The right voted for the tariffs and would vote for them again — and is watching the skilled fab jobs go to imported Taiwanese engineers because nobody built the workforce pipeline that would have made reshoring reshore to American workers.

RD.text: The right is wrapping a regressive consumption tax in nationalist language, claiming vindication for an outcome industrial policy produced and demanding the wall around the economy be built the same way the wall on the border is.

blindAuthoring.authorNote:
The hard part was keeping the centers close without letting them blur — in this window all four stations really are arguing the same paragraph with the same numbers, and the honest rendering is convergence in the middle, not four corners.
The z's surprised me at the rim. I expected the rims to sign by station and they signed by holder: A, B and C all land negative for three different reasons that turn out to be one reason, and D lands at +0.85 on the identical observation that makes B land at −0.45.
That inversion is the actual finding here, and it is why I called the topology a peel rather than an axis split; the lateral fight is real but it is a center phenomenon.
B-fluid was the tempting place to cheat — it would be easy to write the free-trade conservative as a strawman objecting to tariffs on principle, when the live position in January 2026 is reading the thing as a contract and approving of the terms.
I put prevalentAxis on x because the diatribe cells run left/right and the stated object is a protective proclamation, which sits on that line; y would have been the more interesting cleavage and that is exactly why I didn't pick it.
The rim I trust least is A's. There is a version of the institutional left in this window that reaches the rim and signs positive — takes the capacity and shrugs at the signature — and I chose the resentful version because the CHIPS authorship is fresh and the $6.6 billion is theirs. Could be wrong by half a point.
C-fluid I'm confident about; the duty-free clause is the part of this document nobody on television read out loud.

z.pos: the fabs get built and filled — 40 percent of Taiwan's chipmaking actually moves here, Fab 2 tools this year and runs volume in 2027
z.neg: the tariff is a toll nobody pays and the deal is paper — the duty-free window carries the imports, and nothing moves but the announcement

fluid.text: Look at what the exemptions actually do: they let the demand keep flowing while the supply relocates, which is the only way you get from a tenth of our own chips to something real without browning out the data centers. The CHIPS award put the first Arizona fab on 4-nanometer in 2024, Fab 2 is built and tools this year, Fab 3 is going up and Fab 4 is in permitting. That's a build schedule, not a press release.
fluid.zReason: Concrete, dated, physical milestones already cleared — a fab standing in Arizona and a tooling date — outweigh doubts about the legal instrument bolted on top of them.

instrument.holder: the CHIPS appropriation and the fab schedule — Congress's money, TSMC's concrete

coalition.text: We wanted this capacity and we spent four years appropriating for it, so yes, I'll take the fabs. But a tariff with eight exemptions isn't a tariff, it's a lever, and the ninety-day report and the promised Phase 2 are where the actual rates live — none of which is appropriated, obligated, or reviewable. I can want the buildings and still say the enforcement mechanism is an IOU.
coalition.zReason: Splits the ledger: the concrete already funded will deliver, the part resting on proclamation and a future report probably won't, and the net comes out near zero.

instrument.holder: the President, by proclamation, over a Congressional appropriation

denominated.text: We wrote the statute, funded the fabs and awarded the $6.6 billion, and he signed a proclamation and called it his. The deal is whatever he says it is on any given morning.
denominated.zReason: A holder-verdict: what one man can grant by signature he can revoke by signature, so nothing signed this way counts as delivered to us.

fluid.text: Read it as a contract and it's coherent: the 25 percent is the penalty clause, the 15 percent cap is the consideration, and the 2.5x duty-free allowance is what makes building here cheaper than not building here. Taipei put $250 billion of private capital and $250 billion of sovereign credit behind it. You don't get terms like that from a memorandum of understanding.
fluid.zReason: The incentive structure points the same direction as the capital: firms that build get paid to build, firms that don't get charged, and half a trillion is already committed on paper with signatures on it.

instrument.holder: the two governments, as parties to a contract

coalition.text: I want the capacity here and I'll say plainly that the leverage worked — but the Court heard argument in November on whether any of these emergency tariffs were ever his to impose, and it hasn't ruled. You can't underwrite a twenty-year fab against an authority that might be void by summer. Put it through Congress and I'll stop hedging.
coalition.zReason: Believes the economics deliver and the legal foundation might not; a pending ruling on the enforcement authority discounts the whole package to roughly a coin flip.

denominated.text: Twenty-five percent, eight exceptions, and a phone call decides which one you're in. That isn't trade policy, that's a man setting prices.
denominated.zReason: A holder-verdict from the rule-of-law side: discretionary instruments deliver to whoever is in the room, and we are not reliably in the room.

fluid.text: Read the duty-free clause: while you're building, you can bring in two and a half times your planned capacity without paying a cent. So for the next several years the chips still come from Taiwan, and the fab is the permission slip. I'll believe the jobs when there's a project labor agreement on Fab 3, not a groundbreaking photo.
fluid.zReason: The mechanism most likely to be used in the near term is the import allowance, not the construction — the buildings may come, but the clause pays you to wait.

coalition.text: We want those fabs in Phoenix, we've wanted them since 2020, and our locals did the dirt on the first one. But there is not one word in $500 billion about wages, and the last build came with imported crews and a fight over who was qualified. Forty percent of Taiwan's chipmaking is a number about Taiwan; nobody wrote down a number about us.
coalition.zReason: The capital commitment is real but nothing in the instrument routes it to labor, and the prior build is the evidence — delivery to the firms is not delivery to us.

instrument.holder: the firms and the two governments; labor is not a party

denominated.text: Two governments and a chip company divided up half a trillion dollars in two days, and not one person in that room works a shift. They'll build it here and we'll still be asking to get in the door.
denominated.zReason: Holder-verdict: the instrument is held by parties that have never delivered to this constituency, so scale of the number is irrelevant to whether any of it lands here.

instrument.holder: two governments and a chip company

fluid.text: Nine months of investigating and then he signs it and it's law at midnight — and the next morning Taipei is at the table putting up $250 billion of their own money and guaranteeing $250 billion more. The Secretary said it on television: forty percent of their chipmaking moves here. Thirty years of people telling us leverage doesn't work, and it took him a day and a half.
fluid.zReason: Delivery is read off the speed and the counterparty's response — they folded in twenty-four hours, which is proof the pressure is real and will keep being applied.

coalition.text: Best trade day we've had in years, and I'll still say it: eight exemptions is how this town writes a tariff. Data centers are exempt — so the people building the AI warehouses pay nothing and it's the rest of us waiting on Phase 2. Give me Phase 2 at a real rate and I'll take back every word.
coalition.zReason: Trusts the man and distrusts the drafting; expects something to arrive but suspects the carve-outs already routed the good part to somebody else.

instrument.holder: the President, but the drafting is the town's

denominated.text: He holds the pen and the ninety-day clock, and Taipei knows it. It gets built.
denominated.zReason: Holder-verdict with the sign flipped: the discretion that makes every other rim distrust the instrument is exactly what makes this one certain it delivers.

LF.text: The left reads the eight exemptions as sequencing — keep the buyers supplied while the supply relocates — and points at Fab 2 tooling this year as the part of the object that is made of concrete rather than paper.

LC.text: The left narrows to what the instrument omits: no wage floor in $500 billion, no appropriation behind Phase 2, and a 2.5x duty-free window that pays a firm to keep importing while it breaks ground.

LD.text: The left's rim drops the chips entirely and returns a verdict on the holder — our statute, his signature, their room — with no argument attached and none offered.

RF.text: The right reads the object as a contract with a penalty clause, pricing the 15 percent cap against the 25 percent and finding the $250 billion plus $250 billion a fair exchange for it.

RC.text: The right holds two things at once — the leverage worked and the authority may be void — hedging the whole package against a November argument the Court still hasn't answered, while the base hedges instead against the carve-outs.

RD.text: The right's rim splits on the same fact rather than on the object: one side says a man setting prices is not policy, the other says a man setting prices is precisely why it will get built.

window.why: The object formed over two days: the Section 232 chip tariff was signed 01-14 and took effect 01-15, and the US–Taiwan agreement it was written to enforce was signed 01-15, the same day TSMC gave its Arizona guidance and Lutnick said '40 percent' on CNBC. The tariff without the deal is half an object. §4c clause 3: declared at authoring, before any z.

split.seam: between the instrument and the hand holding it — almost nobody in the window disputes that fabs in Arizona are good; they dispute whose proclamation this is and who it will be aimed at next.
split.rationale: At the center all four stations argue the same object with the same facts: eight exemptions, the 2.5x duty-free allowance, $250 billion plus $250 billion, Fab 2 tooling this year. The stations are close in there — the fight is technical and the sides borrow each other's arguments. It is only outward that the object peels away: by the rim nobody is talking about semiconductors at all, only about a man with a pen and a Court that hasn't ruled. The split is radial before it is lateral, which is why strength sits above a half and not near one.

zPattern.note: The rims sign almost purely by holder. Three stations reach the rim and conclude nothing will be delivered to them, because of who is holding it; D reaches the rim and concludes everything will be delivered, for exactly the same reason. The holder is the whole variable out there — the same 25 percent, the same eight exemptions, and a spread of 1.65 on delivery. In the centers the spread is only 0.9 and it tracks the facts instead of the man.

antiValentRationale: At the rim the 25 percent, the exemptions and the fabs are all gone; what remains is a verdict about whose signature is on the page and whether the Court will let it stand.

objectLayer.stated: A 25 percent tariff on advanced foreign computing chips, in force at midnight, to force semiconductor manufacturing back to a country that makes about a tenth of the chips it uses.
objectLayer.operative: A duty almost no American buyer pays — data centers, research, startups, repairs, consumer devices, civil industry and government are all outside it — whose live provisions are the carve-outs and the 2.5x duty-free import allowance for anyone with a fab under construction; that is, a bilateral investment contract with Taipei, carrying a penalty clause that exists mainly to make the contract signable.
objectLayer.inversion: Full sign flip: stated as a barrier to importing chips, operative as a license to import them duty-free at two and a half times capacity, on condition that you are also building. The object travels from roughly +48 to roughly −30 on the same axis — from protection against a foreign supplier to a subsidized channel for that supplier's output.
